review:
Are you old? Did you play a stupid flash game called Motherload in the early 2000s, where you had a crappy mining ship, dug your way down to hell, and fought the devil at the end?

What if you could play a version of that game that was actually good? One with audio that's not awful, with actual artistic intention, and with real game mechanics instead of... whatever that old stuff was?

Now you can. It's called Dome Keeper. It's Motherload, but actually good. And yes, you can also just go play Motherload, the internet still has it lying around. But remember: Dome Keeper costs money while Motherload is free... and both games are worth exactly what you paid for them.

As of 12/8/22 with 207 hours played, I have mixed feelings about this game. On one hand, it started out as a lot of fun and I've clearly spent a ton of time playing it. On the other hand, it's changing rapidly, there's no in-game explanation of changes, and I'm not sure why, but ever since the last big update, I find myself on the wrong end of RNG over and over and over again.

The relic mode is a fun introduction to the game, but you rapidly find yourself realizing that if you're ever going to have fun with all of these other abilities you could theoretically get or gadgets you could max out, you need to play on a bigger stage, so the map size gets bigger and the difficulty gets harder and it didn't take long before I was able to beat a huge map on most difficult setting, and I STILL didn't feel like I was really getting to enjoy ALL of the abilities. So I looked to prestige mode for my time when I wanted to chill and dig some holes.

Some of these runs in prestige have been a great time, and others have just become an annoying slog. In some runs, the waves of monsters are inexplicably more difficult than in other runs (enemies are more numerous right from the first wave, and they appear on opposite ends at the same time), or the rocks are thicker and I can't find iron, then I finally do and crack open a bunch of duds, frequently getting just 1 iron. Also, does every run still yield a hidden room with a seed? I can't tell if it's just that on some runs I'm not finding it and am instead finding the new rooms, or if they're all always in there and it's just a big dig site. Or are they switched up depending on the planets? If so, it would be nice if there was something other than the aesthetic to differentiate these planets, like a planet name somewhere on the screen or some kind of indication so that the people who aren't pulling up faqs or steam guides can also be clued in. I don't think it's hand-holding to provide some of this basic info somewhere.

In terms of gameplay, it seems like whenever there's a gadget with 3 options (thinking shield or repellent), there's always one path that's clearly better than the other 2 paths. Why not just have that path instead of offering wayward options that yield poorer results if you aren't going to make those other options any better?

There's a new alternative to the engineer that I haven't gotten myself to be willing to try out yet because I've invested so much time into the engineer.

There are a lot of random "game modes" and options that are clearly intended to inject more life and staying power into this game. It's just a shame there isn't a campaign mode with missions or "planets" so the developers could offer the player passive exposure to different modes and relics and things while they work through the campaign. Instead we find ourselves becoming entrenched in specific ways of doing things and we have zero incentive to try out these modes that make the game more difficult and yet don't offer any reward.

I also think the game could use some streamlined mechanics to inspire different upgrade pathways. For example, what if the game rewarded the player for following through one upgrade path without altering it by giving cheaper upgrades in that path unless the player deviates? For example, a player could get the basic lvl 1 upgrades they always get, but then they can decide to just focus on their laser until it's maxed out, or they want to max out speed so they can move around super fast, and this is benefited by slightly cheaper upgrades or even by offering to allow water to take the place of 2 irons each or some such thing whenever a player remains in a focused upgrade pathway.

The WORST THING in this game... bar none... is the Teleporter gadget. It breaks the game. I avoid it and turn it into cobalt now because the game is no fun with this damn thing. The game is all about zipping around a cave, digging, and dragging stuff around. That's where most of the fun is found. Why build a gadget that wholesale destroys these gameplay elements and allows the players to completely ignore what are considered ESSENTIAL speed and carry upgrades with any gameplay style that doesn't involve the teleporter? If I was the game developer, I would highlight all the code that has to do with this damn gadget and press delete. Easy choice.

A few closing random thoughts:
1) It's too bad there's no gadget or minor ability that tells you "you need to head back this instant or you're going to be too late" or any other way besides the repellent to get more time in the dig phase (if there is another, I don't know about it. Is that my fault?).

2) There are multiple abilities that nobody gets (inventory display and wave indicator). This was recently changed to where they now cost water instead of iron. Still can't afford to get them, even when I have a water abundance, unless I'm playing in relic mode. Why not quit dicking around with these and just remove them as pay abilities and grant them to the character at the start? We're never going to spend our precious resources on these so you as may as well allow us to have them since you bothered to develop them. They would be NICE to have. They're just not worth the resources.

3) I don't think there's a single gadget that doesn't need either one expensive (for early game) upgrade or several inexpensive upgrades before it's ANY good at all. This is really annoying for prestige mode. I'd rather something take up both gadget spots in my dome than pick something that needs those precious early resources in order to get going. Incidentally, the only option for most gadgets in prestige mode is to turn them into cobalt and gobble them up.

All in all I liked the game a lot, and would have shouted nothing but praise if you caught me in my first 100 hours. As it stands, I'm a little irritated with the game lol since it feels like it's actually gotten worse rather than better since I started playing it. Still going to give it a recommend as it's a great casual game for at least a while. For me right now though, speaking as a laser player... I'm thinking I need to find another game to play when I'm looking to chill. I'll check back after a few months or a year or so and see if it's improved.

A brilliant gameplay loop makes [i]Dome Keeper[/i] a perfect roguelike—for the right kind of player.  Don't be fooled into expecting a relaxing mining experience out of this job; every underground excursion is conducted with one eye on your watch as you hastily carve out and collect your findings before returning to the surface chamber just in time to fight off a fresh wave of shadowy beasts intent on ousting you from your invasive venture.  As the machinery within your dome eagerly grinds up the backbreaking resources you've hauled in, you slump in front of the nearby console for a quick rest and decide whether to invest your iron in improved defensive lasers or a superior drill before getting back on the clock and back in the dirt.  At least down there you're safe.

[i]Dome Keeper[/i]'s beating heart lives in the tension between mining and defense.  You are continuously being drawn back and forth across these roles—rhythmically, predictably, like a pendulum—with your seat at the upgrade/battle terminal serving as a neatly connective transition point between the two sides of the game as one fuels the other.  Everything you do has a touch of tactility and weight and nuance, from the drag of the ore slowing down your jetpack to the need to visit a recharge station for your pulse scanner to the design choice of having wandering orbs pull your misbegotten goods up the lift rather than just letting them float up some boring beam.

The soft pixel art is muted and moody, and the fanfares and periodic ambient melodies of the soundtrack are wistful and warm; alien but inviting.  The more time you spend in the tunnels and caverns, the more they begin to feel like home.  Maybe you'll move in—after you've finished your conquest, of course.

First off: Get this in a sale. imho, this game is not worth the full price for what it is right now. Most negative reviews you see are because of the price since that is to high for what is on offer. Disregarding it's price, for what this game tries to be though, it is a fun game

The game's presentation is great with nice moody backgrounds, good looking effects, atmospheric music and satisfying sound effects. Everything is crisp and snappy. Controls are good/decent and the game-play is nice for a quick game-session. The upgrading is also satisfying and there are a few nice bonus things to find like a stun laser, a creature that digs for you etc.

However; the game-play is also somewhat limited and the loop gets samey. You will quite quickly feel like you experienced everything and new stuff you find/unlock after that is nothing wild or crazy. During a single round the different bonus equipment you can find are quite limited which means there is not much variety during play. Add to that the limited enemy variety and after a few minutes playing you will feel like you are  not really progressing anymore. This would hardly matter for a <10 dollar game that you play in a quick burst between something else, but not for it's full price atm.

Get it on sale and you will enjoy it. Get it for full price and feel like maybe you could have gotten some other game for the same price with more depth.

Alternatives are games like Vampire Survivors or Dig-N-Rig (not on Steam)

It's fun... for about one to two runs. And even then it's not that great. 

The main problem is that the core loop is simply not that interesting. The game tries its hardest to squeeze the absolute maximum fun out of it, but there's only so much water you can squeeze out of a rock. Digging seems like it should be fun, but the maps are rather empty, especially the larger ones. Mostly just rock. Yes, there is ore, upgrades and other fun stuff to find, but it's entirely possible to go an entire cycle without finding anything at all. And even if you do find something, it's probably going to be a pittance anyway, and you'll have to carry it all back (or not, if you have certain upgrades). I don't know; I like mining in games - a lot, in fact - but here it felt frustrating rather than fun.

And the combat isn't much better. The default laser dome can do only one thing: rotate the laser and shoot. You can buy an active skill, which will either damage incoming melee enemies or reflect projectiles - but they can't really be relied upon, they're more like "once-a-wave little helper". The enemies seem like they offer some variety - there's quite a few types - but I don't know, it all just boils down to "keep firing until they pop". No matter if it's a small rhino-type dude, a floating mass of... something, or a hulking, slow-moving monstrosity. Later on I found one enemy that actually felt different - some kind of teleporting wraith - but for the most part combat felt like a slog.

So why did I play for 5 hours? Like I said, the early runs are fun, when you're still learning what is possible. After every successful run you get to unlock a new loadout - a new character (there's only one so far), a new type of dome (again, only one), a new game mode (ditto), different gadgets (there's more actually!). And I tried them out, but they don't really change all that much, and they don't solve the main issue - that the gameplay loop simply isn't that engaging. The sword dome is pretty cool at least, even if it feels unwieldy.

Also, the game has this... polish. It looks fantastic, there's a lot of little things that make the world feel alive - critters, plants growing, cool little hidden powerups such as a speed boost or a helper that carries your loot back to your base. And the soundscape, wow. It's really good - including the music. This feeling of being stranded on a mysterious world with only the walls of your dome protecting you from unknown danger is delicious, even if it fades away after a while.

AAA games have been sacrificing their depth and playability in favour of visual polish for a very long time, and now they're too expensive to make and boring to play at the same time. It's troubling to see the same trend happening in the indie world, too - and we're falling for it all over again. Or maybe I'm just reading too much into it and this is just a game that I personally didn't enjoy.

This is an absolute gem of a game that has devs who are committed to listening to community feedback and actively improving the game post-launch. 

I saw that there was a new massive update and thought, "Wow! That looks awesome... but why isn't it showing up in the store's DLC page?" Well that's because this massive boon to the game's replayability is absolutely FREE. 

I'm sure there will be plenty of other reviews that cover the gameplay side of things, I just wanted to gush at how much I've seen this game improve since launch. In an era where games are being talked about more as products, Dome Keeper sticks out as a passion project from days gone by.

I'd recommend this game to anyone.

It's an incredibly satisfying game and a ton of fun to figure out! The art and sound design are really stunning. It reminds me of the simple fun of Flash games but juiced up with really high production values and a pretty interesting strategic layer.

A note on replayability: Even though it has a roguelike structure, it plays more like a strategy game single-player campaign. You'll have a lot of fun figuring out how to rise to each challenge level, how to play with the different combinations of gadgets, how to macro and micro better. Eventually you'll hit a point where you feel like you "beat" the game and there's not too much more interest in it. (There is a highscore mode, but to me it just feels like a grind, because runs are ultimately pretty similar - there's not really that combinatorial-explosion infinite depth you see in many roguelikes.)

I don't agree with all the reviews saying "you've seen all there is within a couple of hours". You don't even unlock most of the gadget upgrade trees in the first couple of hours let alone discover all the synergies between the relics. You definitely don't get to see all the monsters in one run since they mix and match the variety

But there's still tons the devs could, and do plan to, add to the game to improve variety. Sometimes RNG with the relics can screw you over hard and not give you stuff that works together at all but most relics have functions that help you out greatly once they're upgraded. I'm also looking forward to more characters being added because while the single drill character is fun, the planned one sounds even better. I really hope they support the game for a good while cause there's a really good framework for a lot of variety in upgrades, monsters, characters and cosmetics

But the game is still fun enough and addictive in that you always want to try one more round and push your limits. I found my limit soon enough but I'm hoping I can unlock more upgrades to win some more rounds

This game was on my wishlist for a long time and with the free major update in Juli 2024 I finally bought it.
And oh boy was it worth it.
The game is very polished and coherent in its style and mechanics.
It is overall very well executed.

It gives players a lot of small micro decision to make, like 
- do I drill left, or right, or down, What pattern is efficient, what is most fun?
- when do I return to the dome, do I risk coming back late by drilling too long or carrying too much stuff slowing me down? Greed will be your downfall at least once!
- which monster do I need to target first to minimize damage to my precious dome?

This gives me as the player power and responsibility and feels rewarding because of it.
I never had the feeling the game is unfair, because in the end all my tiny decisions led to the outcome I got.

Every small action is satisfying, like

Dome Keeper is one of those games that pulled me in immediately. It genuinely feels like it was made for the Steam Deck.

I’m playing it on a Steam Deck OLED in docked mode on an external Asus ZenScreen 1080p OLED Screen at stable 60 FPS. In this setup the game runs flawlessly, looks razor sharp, and remains perfectly readable at all times.

The visuals don’t reinvent the wheel, but they are clean, intentional, and highly functional. From the main menu to the in-game UI, the information flow is excellent. Everything is easy to read, nothing feels cluttered, and there are no unnecessary distractions.

At its core, Dome Keeper is easy to describe:
Mining game meets tower defense.

You land on an alien planet with your dome. Mine resources, manage them wisely, buy upgrades, and defend your dome against incoming waves. That’s the gameplay loop - and it works surprisingly well.

The three resources - water, iron, and cobalt - are not explained in depth. At first this feels slightly cryptic, but it actually fits the game’s sense of discovery. It doesn’t hold your hand, and that works in its favor.

I mostly play Relic mode and choose between the four map sizes, from small to huge. Thanks to procedurally generated maps, each run feels unpredictable. Even though you’re technically doing the same thing every time, Dome Keeper does an excellent job of hiding repetition.

The difficulty is fairly scalable, making it accessible for newcomers while still offering a challenge for experienced roguelike players. Different domes, gadgets, and upgrade paths provide enough variety to keep things interesting.

The soundtrack is atmospheric and slightly melancholic. Despite attack waves and time pressure, the game creates an almost meditative mood. That contrast is what makes it special: it’s essentially stress management - yet it feels surprisingly relaxing.

After five hours of playtime, I’m genuinely impressed. If you enjoy roguelikes, chances are very high that you’ll enjoy Dome Keeper as well.

Clear recommendation.

The most important element of a game is the primary gameplay loop, which is what you do most often in a game. If a game has a good gameplay loop, much can be forgiven. If a game doesn't, it could be the most beautiful game ever and still feel lackluster. Dome Keeper's gameplay loop is simple, yet addicting and frankly genius. First, you mine materials and special stuff I won't spoil underground, but be careful, you are on a time limit. When monsters attack you have to quickly rush back to the surface and defend your base, using the materials you mined to help defend against the increasingly dangerous enemy attacks.

The first thing that impressed me about the gameplay loop is the combination of turret base defense and mining. Both have been done, but I am unaware of a combo like this existing before, and how it was missed for so long is sort of surprising given how well they work together. The problem with pure mining games is there is little tension, and trips back to the surface are only for banking your minerals, they are really just there to pad gameplay time. The problem with turret defense games is there is only tension. Fighting waves of enemies until you die to get the highscore is great for an arcade, but not great if you want to make a game that people want to play for hours at a time.

Combining the two, you get a very pertinent reason to travel to the surface (you are going to die if you don't defend) and a great way to get upgrades, through mining. In every action there is a tradeoff, from perfectly timing the length of your mining underground vs being ready to defend before the attacks start, or in the attack vs defense vs mining vs speed upgrades, long term plans vs short term need. Tradeoffs are so important to allowing creativity in a game, and this game is chock full of them.

The only downside to this game is there isn't enough of it! I want more upgrades and secrets. Luckily there are already alternate game characters and upgrades that aren't released yet, and this type of game makes it comparatively simple to add extra stuff.

Even given that caveat, I haven't been this into a roguelike since [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/881100/Noita/]Noita[/url]. If this game could add a fraction of the extra content/random stuff that game has, I'd be very happy.

the beauty of dome keeper is that there are no prerequisites. you don’t need to be in the zone or firing on all cylinders; it’s always there for a quiet 30-minute run, no questions asked.

a game whose depth is revealed gradually, almost sneakily. you’re stranded on an alien planet, your dome is the only thing keeping you alive, and waves of monsters are on their way. between attacks, you drill down into the earth in search of resources like iron, cobalt, and water, bring them back up, and spend them on upgrades. then the next wave hits. then you do it again.

every second you spend underground is a second you’re not at your dome’s controls. do you push deeper for the better materials, or play it safe and head back early? that risk-reward pull never really goes away, and it keeps every run feeling alive even when you’re technically doing the same things over and over.

the roguelike elements help a lot here. each run is procedurally generated, gadgets and upgrades vary, and there’s a meta-progression system that lets you bring permanent perks into future runs. it doesn’t reinvent the wheel, but it’s well-tuned; you feel like you’re getting better at the game and getting a stronger character at the same time. as you keep playing, you unlock new domes, new worlds, new shields; each one comes with its own fun twist that actually changes how you approach a run. each new addition makes you think differently, experiment with new strategies, and find a new favourite setup all over again.

it’s also worth mentioning how atmospheric the game is for something so small. the crash-landing setup, the lonely planet, the sense that you’re just trying to survive long enough to get out. it works.

the latest updates allows you to defend and mine together with friends, and this is honestly where the game has resonated with me the most personally. there’s a particular kind of joy in coordinating with someone, one of you drilling deep while the other holds down the dome. it breathes new life into an already great game.

I’d usually be in favour of waiting for a sale, but at $17.99, it doesn’t really drive a hard bargain to get it at full price.

Dome Keeper is a mining game meshed with elements of old classics like Paratrooper, Load Runner and Brick Breaker. You play the keeper of a dome on a hostile planet. The game play is split into defending your dome against waves of aliens, and mining for resources underneath your hatch. Visually both activities are pixel perfect, the feedback on the screen is great. The controls with a keyboard are simple and sufficient. It's easy to get into a rhythm playing Dome Keeper, keeping the pace, and suddenly forget you've been playing for hours.

When you begin under a new dome, the first steps are to upgrade your dashboard, mining iron, water and cobalt. A good game is a game where mining is done quickly avoiding harder rocks to mine. The mining game is simple, with these 3 primary resources, you'll need to find gadgets and relics in one of two gaming modes. The dome offers upgrades for the various tools and defenses used.

Relic hunting is the first game mode, where a game ends when you bring back the unique relic hidden on the map. Prestige is the second mode, which involves lasting as long as possible against the waves of aliens attacking your dome. Defending in Dome Keeper is done with various weapons against a good variety of alien behaviors. Aliens attacking your shelter change depending on the map randomly selected when you start a game.

Currently, you have the choice between defending with a laser dome or a dome equipped with a sliding shield/sword combination. Both configurations are well balanced against the waves of baddies. I've never made it past wave 52 on relic hunt with the Sword dome. Both profiles have a good set of upgrade choices which you'll want to try on alternate games. There are very little flaws with the game mechanics, everything is easy to figure out on your own, which is great.

This is a fun game to play! There may be improvements to be made on the map generation, some of the sprites could use better defined models, but overall this game is very easy to recommend full price or otherwise.

I loved this game up until I started repeatedly experiencing PowerPoint syndrome while playing the Endless mode in Prestige. The frame rate drops severely during battle after around wave 35 and it becomes unplayable. I love that the devs keep updating the game with more content, but please, do some optimizations. I don't need a new dome or keeper, I just need the game to be playable. Losing a great run because it turned into a presentation is one of the worst experiences in a game.

Another complaint I have (which is rather minor compared to the poor optimization) is that sometimes the color palettes don't help at all. On some of the paler colored worlds, I can hear a Diver coming, but there's very little contrast between the warning particles/animation and the world's color background, and I'm left guessing which side the Diver is going to come from. Same goes for the aiming lines for the Artillery dome, sometimes it's hard to see where I'm aiming when the contrast between the line and the background is low. Maybe it's my aging vision, or maybe the colors look too pale, or maybe it's the low frame rate when there are so many monsters on the screen. Most likely it's all of those things combined. My vision isn't going to change, but I really do think an in-game option to adjust color contrast would be very welcome by many. Or at least stroke outlines. The devs were diligent and caring enough to include a few accessibility options, so why not look into this as well?

Other than that, the game is fun. Testing new builds for Prestige is fun. The challenges are fun (need more of those!) and the music fits perfectly. It just needs optimization. Even thematically the game is interesting. I would write an essay on how it could be interpreted to be about ecocide and indigenous resistance, and how the dome keeper is actually the villain, but that's not the focal point of my review.

I was quite looking forward to this release actually, and there's a lot of good to it, but at the same time, some, in my opinion glaring flaws that ultimately stop this game from being enjoyable. Let's start with what's done excellently. 

The general quality and polish of the game is fantastic, the art is stunningly beautiful and really quite cute! There're a lot of little details here and there in the animations of the various pieces of the dome that make it come alive, and you can get little pets that hang around your dome. The atmosphere as well is brilliantly captured. The soundtrack helps to make you really feel the tension of crash landing on an alien world with hostile locals that are [i] not [/i] happy about your presence. It really does feel like I'm playing a Metroid game in certain ways that are just perfect. That feeling and atmosphere of exploring an alien landscape, or in this case, alien mine, is perfectly captured. And it's exemplified by the general polish and feeling of the graphics, soundtrack, and best of all, controls. Which are again, finely tuned and feel great to play with. The controls lend themselves to the simplistic nature of the game, you simply run into the blocks you want to mine to break them, which to me, was quite a joy and innovative. And I loved the little jingles and unique sounds each ore makes as you mine them / pick them up, etc. Attention to detail like that is great! So yeah, there's a lot of really solid base here that makes it really shine in some ways. 

Now for what I have issues with. Honestly, it feels like there's a lot of anti-fun design in the game. If you're looking for a relaxing experience where you're super over-powered and blow through all the enemies, or you get this game and are waiting for that moment to happen, then in my opinion, this is not the game. That moment of crazy over-poweredness never came for me. And I don't think it ever would, that's not what the game is trying to be. It's always a race against the clock to collect more resources and complete the objective  before you inevitably die. It feels like the game is too much of a resource / time scramble to really be fun. Sometimes you'll get really unlucky and find no resources where you choose to dig, and it basically ends your run. Not to mention how expensive the later upgrades are. And most of the upgrades feel so bad that it feels pointless to get them. They sound really good on paper, like "oh wow! I got a resource elevator that will ferry resources for me!" Or "Oh, now I can teleport anywhere I want!" Until you realize that both of them are so restricted in their use, or take so many resources through upgrades to be useful, it almost feels like they're not even there. I saw some early release footage from some YouTubers and some upgrades have been changed to make the game even harder than it honestly feels like it needs to be. There's one particular resource, cobalt, that you generally use to repair your dome, but it's so hard to find, and you'll generally always take damage due to the nature of how scarce resources are, that you are basically pigeon holed into using them to repair, always, which really isn't fun. That's the whole thing, you might look at the upgrade paths and be like "wow! There are so many different ways to play! So many different upgrades!" But the amount of resources you're able to find and the high cost of each upgrade, in tandem with the overwhelming force of the enemy after even just a few waves, culminates in the player practically being forced to choose a certain path of upgrades, or die otherwise. Those upgrades being character mining speed, resource carry speed, and weapon damage. As such, you never really have time to play around with the more "fun" upgrades the game has to offer, and the experience ends up feeling more like a claw to the finish rather than a relaxing, fun delve into the depths of the planet for resources. Of course, if you enjoy that kind of oppressing feeling of being pushed to your limit and stressed, putting out fires, then I'm sure you'd enjoy it quite a bit, but I didn't find it enjoyable. And this is coming from someone that has played over 150 hours of Factorio, where you similarly have to put out fires against an unstoppable force. To me, all of these reasons combined make the experience feel like it has an anti-fun design. Personally, I'd make resources more plentiful, or easier to transport back to your dome and make the various artifact upgrades you can find more relatively powerful, given how hard they can be to even find in some runs. Just in general make the upgrades more meaningful / impactful, if they're going to be so costly, they need to really feel like they're worth the cost. 


Either way, I do quite enjoy it for what it is though. And I do still think it's worth a play if you get it on the cheap, as others are saying, just for the fact of the level of polish, and it certainly is fun to go mining for different ores! So it'll certainly scratch that itch for you, if for but a moment. And again, all that said, this is just my opinion, and I'm not trying to be too harsh to the great work the developer has put in. I certainly couldn't make something this good. Thanks for reading, hope this helps someone!

[h3]Impeccable vibes. Not much content[/h3]

The atmosphere alone sells this game. The pixel art, the animations, the phenomenal soundtrack, the sound effects in general, even the subtle story elements. All of it is so detailed yet understated, and so full of character. This game has vibes.

The gameplay itself alternates in waves between being a simple horde-defender type game, and a "Motherload"-like 2D mining game, with some soft roguelite elements like. It's a simple yet satisfying core gameplay loop, reminiscent of Kingdom.

BY FAR the biggest weakness of this game is the lack of content. Updating this [b]4 years after release[/b] and this game still seems to fall far short of being a real "roguelike". If that's all you're looking for this game might disappoint you a little, as there are only about 10 different gadgets to find and not much other variation to your runs.

As far as replayability, the devs have frustratingly chosen to continue adding modes and characters, rather than expand the existing primary game mode, which is... fine I guess? Pretty much every new mode and character is at best a novelty and at worst a patently inferior experience compared to the base game. It's a shame, because if that time and energy went into adding new gadgets or discoverable objects, then the base game would've increased exponentially. But on the flipside at least the devs have been very supportive of the modding community, which is really nice to see.

All in all, if you like atmosphere and some difficulty, def pick this one up.

Dome Keeper has one of the most satisfying game loops I've played in a long time. Dig for Resources -> Upgrade -> Defend Dome-> Repeat. It's clear a lot of effort and time went into make sure this was the case. I've played for nearly 30 hours and still plan to play a lot more. 

If you've read the negative reviews here on Steam, you'll notice two main criticisms over and over that I want to address. This is despite agreeing to an extent. Those being:

- The game is too repetitive
- There is a lack of content

I think the game is well worth your time and will certainly be well worth your money once more content is added. It is true that the game lacks content at release (but is far from the "unfinished game" comments you'll see around). Most notably, there isn't enough to find while digging and not enough variety in the Gadgets that you can dig up that alter how you might approach things. I believe this is why most people find the game too repetitive despite the gameplay loop itself being very satisfying. The lack of variety just makes it a bit samey sometimes, even with the 4 difficulty levels, 3 run modifiers, 2 types of domes, and 3 types starter Gadgets that currently exist. There's also a few different worlds you can spawn in, but their differences aren't immediately apparent (it's mostly enemy types).

This doesn't mean there isn't depth in the game though, far from it! This become evident in the Score Attack mode named "Prestige" where the depth found in all 3 facets of the game are required to be learned to gain a very good score since it allows you to give up resources (and thus upgrades) for a better score. Even the simple act of digging has more depth than it first appears. During the main "Relic Hunt" mode, these aren't as necessary (Unless you play on "You Asked for it" difficulty), so I can understand why some people may not recognize the depth in the game currently. 

However, it is absolutely satisfying to get better at this game. It is well designed and has great presentation from the artwork and music. It also sounds like the main issues with the game will be ironed out over time as it seems more content is on the way (there is, at the very least, a new character coming). There's a lot of potential here and I can't wait to see what comes of it. 

I certainly recommend Dome Keeper!

[h1]Overview[/h1]

After my first taste of victory on a brutal difficulty, which no doubt there will be more to come, I am ready to share my initial thoughts on Dome Keeper and will update this review as time goes by. Right now, it is a strong recommendation if you enjoy pixel art roguelike action game. The design of the game is good and engaging. You are constantly racing against time. The game is challenging but you will improve as you play and will beat it eventually. It is hard but fair. I don't feel frustrated at all when I lose (which is pretty often).

[h1]Detail Review[/h1]

It is a roguelike action mining game. You are a Dome Keeper, which is also a Relic Hunter. Your dome landed on an alien planet and accidentally squashed one of the indigenous creatures to death. That must have triggered a revenge attack. Your dome is going to undergo waves and waves of attack from various types of creatures. Should you manage to find the relic before the dome collapses, you win. Otherwise, you lose. Come to think on it, that game opening reminds of the movie Avatar.

At brutal difficulty - the intended difficulty for this game - the game is pretty challenging.  There are two levels below for more relax game play and one level up (need unlock) for the veterans. You have to constantly prioritize how to allocate resources to the tech trees that improve yourself, your dome, and your gadgets found in the map. You have to constantly make decision on where to dig and how much to carry during the "peace" phase and which enemy type to take down first during the "war" phase.

Gadgets are game changers and they can dramatically change your strategy and approach to the game. You may carry forward one gadget of your choice from your last game to the next one. You can also find new ones as you explore the map. Gadgets have their own tech trees for improvement. Dome Keeper is a roguelite mining game where the player must find a relic buried deep below the surface of a strange alien world, while waves of increasingly more powerful shadowlike creatures try to destroy your dome.

As you dig deeper underground you’ll need to collect resources and carry them to your dome, which then allows you to purchase upgrades for drill strength, movement speed, dome shield and weapon strength, and special abilities for various gadgets that can significantly alter your tactics.

These gadgets include a bomb which can quickly clear large areas, a probe to scan the nearby area for resources, a lift to carry resources up to your dome, a teleport which can reduce time spent travelling back and forth through deep mines, a dinosaur like creature who can help you mine, and a stun laser which automatically targets enemies during combat.

There are a few different enemy types, including ground based enemies who will try to smash your dome in melee range, and flying enemies who shoot energy bolts from overhead. You can fight enemies with a laser beam or a sword (which can be fired out to hit distant targets), and you could equip a shield to protect from damage, or use repellent to delay enemy waves so you get attacked less often.

While each run takes between 1-2 hours, there’s a good amount of replayability provided by different map sizes and difficulty levels, a second character who has a different mining technique, and a prestige mode where instead of finding a relic you’re chasing a high score earned by sending resources home.

The pixel graphics are basic, but good enough to understand what is happening. I haven’t had any problems with bugs or crashes. The game’s menu says it plays best on gamepad, but I think the keyboard controls work just fine.

Dome Keeper is a simple but fun game which is worth checking out if you’re looking for something a bit different.

It's a game about work.

Domekeeper is game in a class of games where the mundane drudgery of the tasks the game asks of you is indeed the whole reason you play them.

    In Domekeeper's "Relic Hunter" the primary game play mode, you alternate between developing and expanding the mine beneath your dome to find and retrieve a rare alien relic buried there, and coming to the surface to defend your dome from waves of attacks in a pseudo tower defense like combat that is reminscent of Atari classic  Missile Command (1980). These two modes of play often frustrate each other in a delicate tension that creates the most truly engaging moments the game has. The game is at it's best when you are making difficult decsions between investing mined resources into things that will allow you to more efficiently excavate the mine and things that will keep you alive long enough to finish the excavation. Like any good game about resource management you must carefully weigh your short term and long term benefits.
    The game falters however whenever you get too far ahead of the curve and can more trivially extract resources and keep ahead of the needs for upgrades. Their is often a long late game where any steadily increasing difficulty in waves of enemies is easily met by your current weapons upgrades and victory is inevitable but not immenent. Relic Hunter lacks any late game curveballs that can disrupt you once you're on path to victory. Even the final wave of enemies that attack you once you succesfully extract the relic is perfunctory, as you literally cannot lose at that point. Fail to defend the dome and the relic will wipe all the remaining enemies and show you the victory screen. The lack of tension in the later parts of runs is often what makes the game start to feel truly menial
     The alternate challenge modes however are where the game manages to stay interesting once you've found out the basic rhythms and can see through it's tricks. Prestige is a score attack that once again mirrors this games arcade ancestors. Players compete to get the highest score by surviving waves of attacks and sending home the most cobalt. Cobalt being one of the rarest of the 3 primary resources, used for a few upgrades but mostly as the only thing that can repair your dome should you let it be damaged, it's a lifeline for that reason. The game becomes a pure test of skill as you ultimately plan to become more effeciant in your mining than any of your peers.
     "Guild Assignments" offer alternate difficult twists to the classic Relic Hunter Gameplay loop, changing the density of resources, variety of enemies that can attack you and even in some laying out different victory conditions. A personal favourite of mine is "Iron Contribution". In this format there are no enemies atacking your dome, and you don't need to find a buried relic. Instead you must in a relatively tight timeframe set aside a large portion of iron to send away. Meeting the quota is difficult as the tension that brings interest here is iron (One of the 3 primary resources you mine for) is the resource needed to upgrade your capacity to mine more efficiently. You are forced to find the delicate balance between spending all of your iron to extract more iron, and actually having enough left over to send away before the end of your shift. Given more time you would quite easily max out your capacity to produce iron, and then quickly amass it. The tight timeframe however forces you to find out how much is "good enough" to get all the resources you need out in time and actually finish. The sort of practical compromises are where it feels like the more interesting drudgery of doing a real job. If you gave me 4 men, the gadget supplements I wanted, and a starting stipend of iron to max the neccesary skill trees for drilling, carrying and moving I could get you this easy. Alas we are short staffed. You can have 2 stock gadgets and whatever you need for upgrades is gonna have to come out of your own pocket. Oh and did I say I need it in 30? Suddenly you find yourself a slightly overworked mid level employee. The drones you picked as your primary gadget are helping fill the labour gap by carrying the iron ore back to the surface as you mine, so you don't have to waste trips carrying it back and forth yourself. However you quickly find you can mine quicker than they can pick it up and a backlog starts to build up. You can pay to increase the number of drones and most of that cost is in water and not iron so is that a better option over upgrades to make the drones move faster? Meanwhile any large items you find that can help you mine faster still have to hauled up yourself as the drones cant left them. So as you lug a large unidentified gadget or supplement to the surface to install in your dome and hope it's something thats useful you have to hope you have a large enough backlog of iron that needs to be carried that the drones stay occupied the entire time you're away from mining because they can't drill themselves and you don't want them standing around wasting time. And the clock keeps ticking down, you see you're at the halfway mark, decide it's not worth it to even pick up any more gadgets because the base amount of iron you have to invest to get them worthwhile you won't earn back in the time you have left. And you realize now there's a backlog again and you should probably drop what you're doing, put down the drill and just start hauling whatever you have available to the surface because you're gonna run out of time. You start making your way up with as much iron as you can reasonably carry in one trip, every bit slowing you down slightly and realize you're deeper than you thought. You slowly ascend weighing if it's worth it to bring one less ingot to the surface if it lets you get there a bit faster and you might be able to squeeze in 2 trips before your run out of town. It starts to dawn on you as you plod along that you haven't seen any drones in a long damn while and it's starting to feel like you're the only one who works here. And suddenly they pass you carrying ingots one at a time in a slow line to the surface having ignored the bundled ingots you set aside in groups of 4 and 5 for them to carry in favor of lone ingots that were closer to the main drill shaft and made more sense to their programmed pathfinding. All of the sudden this game is everything you hated about the last time your job had "supervisor" in the title and yet you're having a sort of fun. The time runs out, you're 30 iron shy of your quota and when you reach for the coffee it's cold. You hit restart on the level, start over the album in your headphones and wonder if the drones are worth the trouble or if you should just carry the damn ingots yourself next time.

TL;DR: Good concept and artstyle, but feels very incomplete and as a result, tedious

It feels like they had a concept for a really unique base defense game, but instead of fleshing out the endgame they just added a reset button to take you back into the tedious early game. 

At its core, this game is about time management. There's two main gameplay segments, mining and combat. The combat just serves as a pressure mechanic so you can't spend all of your time being productive. When the combat timer ticks down, you have to fly all the way back to the top of your base or else the hostile mobs will destroy you.

The mining starts off slow and tedious, but by the end of a run you will have unlocked enough upgrades that mining is now just tedious. The mining never gets more interesting than strip mining in Minecraft. There is no danger underground. You just hold a single direction until you find a resource, bring it to base, repeat until you find the area's special upgrade.

The special upgrades are the coolest part of the game. You can add special systems like an elevator, teleporter, or digbot to your base. I would really hope upgrades like this would reduce the amount of tedium in mining, but they're usually so unimpactful that they just serve as a minor additional revenue stream instead of something you can adapt your gameplay around. 

The combat is alright. It is a bit challenging at times, but only if you fall behind on the upgrade tree.  There's only 5 or 6 enemy types that I encountered. I can't say the combat is exciting. It feels more like a DPS check than an interesting battle. 

The alternate defense and weapons systems you unlock (there is one of each) by completing a run are also not very good. Either I played them terribly wrong, or they are in severe need of redesigns. They felt vastly inferior to the base loadout in regards to both killing enemies and avoiding damage. 

I feel like there's a decent foundation on which a good game could be built, but as it stands it's just a tad dull. There was never a point where I thought "this is cool!". Just incremental upgrades until the end so I could upgrade my weapon enough to survive the combat sequences.

!!! GADGETS AND DISCOVERIES: I am NOT going to spoil anything here but there are devices you can find called gadgets that will VASTLY help you on your runs and each in a very unique way. And the best part is that you can choose to keep one gadget if you die on a run so it can help you from the get-go on your next run! Not only are there gadgets but there are also some very very cool random things you will discover while you mine that can also help you along your way.

!!! Customizeability : The game has many ways to play and there are options to unlock for larger maps that take longer to play as well as different dome types and ways to defend said dome; AND there are modifiers you can unlock to make the experience more tailored to what you want (My personal favorite is "longer wave timers", it makes the waves of monsters more spaced out but it makes the waves themselves tougher) and so this is really a game you can get into a rhythm with and then play how you like.


My final remarks are that Dome Keeper is a very fun roguelike base-defender that will definitely appeal to you if you like that hypnotizing satisfaction of mining in games like Minecraft and the team who did the sound work for this game deserves an award.
